title: Joining the USO through Dick Campbell
summary: After his father-in-law's death Pillars visits USO talent coordinator Dick Campbell, who signs the band, and they travel to New York by Pullman.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: And my wife's father died. And I left and went to New York to the funeral. While in New York, I decided to go

by and see a fellow named Dick Campbell who was the coordinator of talent for the USO camp shows. I had met Dick when we were playing the Apollo Theater. So I went down to the USO camp shows, and Dick was glad to see me. And he said, "By the way, Pillars, how would you like to come with the USO?" He says, "We'll keep you in the States a few weeks, and then maybe we'll send you to Europe." I said, "It's a good deal." He says, "When can you join the band?" I said, "Well, we're working at the Club Plantation now. Our last night is Labor Day night."

He says, "Okay, I'll tell you what I'll do. I'll book you, put you on the train, we'll get Pullmans for you, put you on the next morning, you'll get on the train, and you'll come on out to New York and we'll process you for USO." Sent us the contract and we signed it. We finished that night, Labor Day night, got on the train the next day, everybody had a lower berth except my wife and I. And I wanted it that way. I told them, I said, "You fellows take the lower berths. My wife and I, we'll take an upper berth." Because I know how adversely the men feel when a man comes in and takes his wife -- takes one of the good berths and leaves a berth like that to one of them, and it might create a little bad sentiment, so I told them to go ahead on and take the lower berths.
So what I did, I saw the conductor passing through, and I spoke with him, I told him, sir, I was travelling with my

wife and she wasn't feeling too well, and it would be hard for her to ride up -- to get up there in the berth. I said, "I'd appreciate it if you could get something better for me." He said, "Well, I'll see what I can do for you." And by the time we had got to Columbus, Ohio, he had -- he gave us a roomette, which I thought was real nice.

And we arrived at New York, met Dick the next day, and he had us to meet him at the Nola Studio. I don't know if the Nola Studio is still active in New York or not, but this is a studio that's down on Broadway, about 54th and Broadway.
Where you did all your rehearsing?

Yeah, rehearsal rooms and recording rooms. And you could just leave your instruments there. You could check them in and leave them there, see. So we just kept our music there while we were rehearsing.
